title: Tool‑Augmented Post‑Processing of Identical LLM Candidates for Intent‑Driven Network Configuration (shared_initial_candidate evaluation)
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1) that isolates the effect of deterministic post‑processing (a NetOps verifier + lightweight topology simulator) on deterministic‑validator pass/fail outcomes when the same single LLM candidate is reused verbatim across conditions (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Planned: 300 paired tasks (600 episodes); completed: 598 episodes → 299 complete pairs. For the 299 analyzable pairs the archived contingency is n11=299, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0; both baseline and guarded arms accepted the identical candidates (299/299). Paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10k resamples, seed=1729). All raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSONs, task manifests, and execution logs are archived with SHA‑256 hashes (see Disclosure). Under the shared_initial_candidate semantics this run shows no downstream‑postprocessing effect on the deterministic validator verdict for identical candidates; it does not answer whether independent tool‑augmented generation would change generation quality or safety.

sections.introduction: Generative LLM‑based pipelines are being proposed to translate operator intent into executable network configurations. Production architectures typically pair a generative model with deterministic validators/simulators and optional repair loops (generate→validate→repair). Evaluations of such systems must separate (A) improvements that originate during generation from (B) effects that arise solely from downstream verification/repair. To isolate (B) we preregistered and executed a paired experiment in which a single shared LLM candidate (the shared_initial_candidate) was produced per task and reused verbatim by both the baseline and guarded pipelines. The primary confirmatory estimand (pre‑registered) is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on a deterministic‑validator binary pass indicator. This manuscript reports the complete, artifact‑anchored preregistered study: design, execution provenance, exact results, statistical assessment, representative validator diagnostics, and limitations.
sections.related_work: Recent NetOps and AIOps literature motivates verifier‑augmented agent designs and intent→configuration research. Representative verified sources that informed our design include work on intent‑driven configuration and LLM translation (Nguyen et al., 2024, doi:10.1002/nem.2313), pretrained configuration models (PreConfig, arXiv:2403.09369), and reports on tool‑augmented agent architectures and runtime reliability (selected recent preprints and system papers summarized in our preregistration and evidence bundle). Prior evaluations often conflate generator improvements with post‑processing effects; our contribution is an artifact‑grounded isolation of the latter using a preregistered paired design and deterministic verifier traces.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand. The study was preregistered as cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1 (preregistration SHA‑256: 991674d51794b41cf66471509149237b9a99f709b69aa3408d3d9d2ea2d50fc0). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on a deterministic‑validator binary pass indicator. Design semantics. We executed the shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each task we produced one LLM candidate and reused it verbatim in both conditions (baseline vs guarded). This design isolates downstream post‑processing effects while holding generator output fixed. Sampling and power. Planned n=300 paired tasks (150 simple, 150 complex). The preregistered power calculation targeted a minimally important paired difference of +0.20 (assumed baseline ≈0.60), α=0.05, power≈0.90. Model, orchestration, and verifier. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json; artifact SHA‑256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). Adapter/orchestrator: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator/simulator used: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version 5.0). Validator behavior: parse candidate commands into canonical configuration, enforce per‑task workflow invariants (e.g., make_before_break, shutdown_configure_restore), compute final_state in a lightweight topology simulator and emit violation codes when invariants are broken. Reproducibility and provenance. All raw LLM responses, provider traces, validator traces, per‑episode scoring JSONs, task manifests, the execution log, and a full SHA‑256 manifest were archived (execution/*). Example authoritative artifact locations (sample): execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (sha256: 8f38c8becd7e1e36...), execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json (sha256: 6569b491...), execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (sha256: cefa6344...). The full per‑file hash manifest is available in the execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json). Missingness, exclusions, and failures. Preregistered exclusions: exact matches to a curated public config corpus (none removed from the confirmatory set). Missingness policy: complete‑pair analysis as primary; sensitivity analyses treating failed runs as verifier‑fail were preregistered. Execution logging captured two failed episodes (failed_episode_count=2) that comprised a single missing pair (pair‑000269); the provider failure event and provider trace are archived in the execution log and provider traces (see Disclosure and execution manifest; execution/execution_log.jsonl SHA‑256: b45a600859502b088a9416744ccbff3f5fba2e6dd76b863440bdfd36ebf21bb8).
sections.results:
Execution summary. Planned episodes: 600 (300 pairs). Completed episodes: 598; failed episodes: 2; analyzable complete pairs: 299. Model call accounting: model_calls_used = 300 (one shared generation per task). Confirmatory contingency (artifact: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 d77df43abf83e081...): n11 = 299, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Baseline success rate = 299/299 (100.0%); guarded success rate = 299/299 (100.0%). Point estimate of paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0 (pre‑registered test). Bootstrap (10k resamples, seed=1729) percentile 95% CI for paired difference = [0.00, 0.00] (degenerate CI because no discordant pairs; artifact: analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg). Representative scored episode (artifact example). Task pair‑000001 (execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt; sha256 8f38c8be...): the shared candidate produced by the LLM was "interface edge1 admin down
interface edge1 vlan 30
interface edge1 mtu 1600
interface edge1 admin up". The deterministic validator parsed and canonicalized the candidate, simulated final_state, and returned valid = true with parsed_command_count = 4 and required_command_count = 4 (see execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json and execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json; sha256s archived). Missingness and failure accounting. The single excluded pair (pair‑000269) corresponds to two failed episodes resulting from a failed shared_initial provider call; the failure event and provider trace are archived in the execution log and provider traces (execution/execution_log.jsonl; SHA‑256 b45a600859502b088a9416744ccbff3f5fba2e6dd76b863440bdfd36ebf21bb8). Per our preregistered plan the pair was excluded from the primary complete‑pair analysis; all failure artifacts are preserved for audit. Ceiling effect and interpretational constraint. Observed baseline success = 299/299 produced a ceiling effect that invalidates the preregistration power assumption (baseline≈0.60). Consequently, the run cannot detect the originally targeted minimally important paired difference of +0.20. We therefore report exact counts and exact McNemar p‑value and explicitly caution that absence of discordant pairs does not provide evidence about tool impact on independently generated candidates.
sections.discussion: Interpretation. Under the strict shared_initial_candidate semantics — the same single LLM candidate reused verbatim by both pipelines — deterministic verifier+simulator post‑processing did not change the deterministic‑validator pass/fail outcome in our confirmatory set (299 concordant accepted pairs). This is a narrow, preregistered answer about post‑processing effect for identical candidates and must not be generalized to claims about tool‑augmented generation. Operational implications. Deterministic validators remain valuable for audit trails, failure codes, and explicit final_state snapshots even when they do not alter a perfect candidate; they are critical when generators err or when independent generation is used. Design lessons for follow‑ups. To measure the operational benefit of tool‑augmented agents on generated outputs, future preregistered studies should (A) use independent per‑condition generation (not shared candidates), (B) include adversarial/harder task strata to avoid ceiling effects, (C) replicate across model families and seeds, and (D) report full provenance and deterministic hashes as here. Threats to validity. Internal validity: shared_initial semantics intentionally remove generator variance but preclude assessing generation improvements that a tool‑augmented agent might induce. Construct validity: the deterministic validator encodes a curated set of workflow constraints (documented per task manifest) and is a reasonable but incomplete proxy for vendor/hardware behavior. External validity: synthetic topologies and vendor‑agnostic CLI fragments limit direct transfer to production vendor CLIs and device idiosyncrasies. Conclusion validity: the observed ceiling (baseline=1.00) prevents detection of the preregistered minimally important effect; we therefore report exact counts and the degenerate bootstrap CI rather than interpreting the run as a powered null.
sections.conclusion: In a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired run that fixed generation (shared_initial_candidate), deterministic verifier+simulator post‑processing did not change deterministic validator pass/fail outcomes: both arms accepted the identical candidates in all 299 analyzable pairs (n11=299). This narrowly scoped finding documents the downstream‑postprocessing effect (or lack thereof) when generation is identical; it does not address whether tool‑augmented independent generation would produce safer or higher‑quality candidates. All execution and analysis artifacts, with SHA‑256 manifests, are archived to enable independent audit and reproducibility.

disclosure_statement: Mandatory Disclosure Statement: This manuscript and all reported results derive from an autonomous post‑lock research run governed by the immutable initial master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). The experiment was preregistered as cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1 and frozen prior to execution (preregistration SHA‑256: 991674d51794b41cf66471509149237b9a99f709b69aa3408d3d9d2ea2d50fc0). Declared LLM used: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json; artifact SHA‑256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). Orchestration/adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (version 5.0). Generation semantics required by the preregistration and executed here: shared_initial_candidate — for each paired task a single LLM candidate was produced and reused verbatim by both the baseline and guarded pipelines. The shared candidate raw response files are archived at execution/responses/task-<NNN>-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256s recorded under execution/*) and the provider call traces for these shared generation events are archived at execution/provider_calls/task-<NNN>-shared-initial.json (see execution manifest for the full per‑file hash list). Execution accounting: planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs); completed episodes = 598; failed episodes = 2 (forming one missing pair, pair‑000269); analyzable complete pairs = 299. The failed shared_initial provider call that produced the missing pair is recorded in the execution log (execution/execution_log.jsonl; SHA‑256: b45a600859502b088a9416744ccbff3f5fba2e6dd76b863440bdfd36ebf21bb8) and in the corresponding provider trace (archived). All raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSONs, task manifests, analysis artifacts, and a full manifest of SHA‑256 artifact hashes are archived and serve as the authoritative source for every reported number (authoritative manifest path: execution/execution_manifest.json). No manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock; all manuscript numeric claims are grounded in these archived execution and analysis artifacts. This run followed the preregistered analysis plan (paired exact McNemar and bootstrap CI) and the missingness/contamination rules; any deviations are recorded in the execution/analysis manifests. The present manuscript reports only the narrowly preregistered estimand (effect of downstream tooling on identical LLM candidates) and explicitly does not claim results about independent tool‑augmented generation without further experiments.
limitations: The executed semantics fixed generation by reusing a single shared LLM candidate per task (shared_initial_candidate); results therefore answer only whether post‑generation tooling changes deterministic validator pass/fail for identical candidates, not whether independent tool‑augmented generation would produce different or safer outputs.
Tasks used deterministic synthetic topology templates and a lightweight simulator; external validity to vendor‑specific CLIs, device‑level idiosyncrasies, or production telemetry is limited.
Only one declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was used; results do not generalize across model families or scales without replication.

The deterministic validator enforces a curated rule set and workflow constraints; it cannot exhaustively model every hardware or vendor behavior and thus is an imperfect proxy for full production correctness.
A ceiling effect occurred: observed baseline success = 299/299, invalidating the preregistered power assumption and preventing detection of the originally targeted minimally important effect.
